questions.topic: Refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: While taking readings with a travelling microscope, the microscope should always be moved in one direction only.
statements.R: The least count of the travelling microscope is found in the same way as for vernier calipers.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: One-directional motion avoids backlash error. The least count method is a separate fact.
steps: A is true: moving in one direction avoids backlash error.
R is true: the least count is found as in vernier calipers.
R does not explain why the movement must be one-directional. Backlash does.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) fail. R is unrelated to backlash, so option (1) fails.
solution.common_trap: Picking option (1) simply because both statements are true.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: If $R_2$ is the reading for the mark seen through the slab and $R_3$ is the reading for powder on its top surface, the apparent thickness of the slab is $R_3 - R_2$.
statements.II: The normal shift $R_2 - R_1$ of the mark is equal to $t/n$, where t is the real thickness of the slab.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Apparent thickness = $R_3 - R_2$, and normal shift = $t(1 - 1/n)$.
steps: Statement I matches the definition of apparent thickness, so it is correct.
The normal shift is $t(1 - 1/n)$. The quantity $t/n$ is the apparent thickness, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II confuses the shift with the apparent thickness, so options (1) and (4) fail. Statement I is correct, so option (2) fails.
solution.common_trap: Treating the apparent thickness $t/n$ as the shift.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: In the forward characteristic of a silicon p-n junction diode, the current stays negligible until the knee voltage is reached. What is the approximate knee voltage?

solution.key_concept: The knee voltage is about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge.
steps: For a silicon diode, the forward current rises steeply beyond about 0.7 V.
solution.why_not_others: 0.3 V is the value for Ge. 1.7 V and 7 V are far too large for a silicon diode.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the Si and Ge values.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: In the forward characteristic of a diode, the current increases from 10 mA to 30 mA when the voltage increases from 0.70 V to 0.75 V. What is the dynamic resistance of the diode in this region?

solution.key_concept: $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$
steps: $\Delta V = 0.05$ V.
$\Delta I = 20$ mA = 0.020 A.
solution.why_not_others: 25 $\Omega$ is the static ratio V/I at 0.75 V and 30 mA. 0.4 is $\Delta I/\Delta V$, the inverse. 70 $\Omega$ is V/I at 0.70 V and 10 mA.
solution.common_trap: Using V/I at a single point instead of the ratio of changes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: When a p-n junction diode is reverse biased, a microammeter records a small, nearly constant current. Which statement correctly describes this current?
options: It is due to minority carriers and increases with temperature
It is due to majority carriers and does not depend on temperature
It is due to minority carriers and does not depend on temperature
It is due to majority carriers and increases rapidly with reverse voltage

solution.key_concept: The reverse saturation current comes from minority carriers and increases with temperature.
steps: In reverse bias, majority carriers are blocked, so only minority carriers drift across the junction.
The number of minority carriers increases with temperature, so this current increases with temperature.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): It is due to minority carriers and increases with temperature
solution.why_not_others: Majority carriers do not carry the reverse current. The current does depend on temperature. Below breakdown it stays nearly constant with reverse voltage.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the reverse saturation current is independent of temperature.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Meter used to measure current in forward bias

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Meter used to measure current in reverse bias

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Knee voltage of a germanium diode

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Reciprocal of the slope of the I-V curve at a point

solution.key_concept: Forward current is of the order of mA, and reverse current is of the order of μA. The Ge knee voltage is about 0.3 V. $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$.
steps: A: forward current is in mA, so a milliammeter is used. A-IV.
B: reverse current is in μA, so a microammeter is used. B-II.
C: Ge knee voltage is about 0.3 V. C-III.
D: the reciprocal of the slope is the dynamic resistance. D-I.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap the two meters or mix up the knee voltage with the dynamic resistance.
solution.common_trap: Using the microammeter in forward bias.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: Which of the following statements about p-n junction diode characteristics are correct?

statements.A: In forward bias, the p side is connected to the positive terminal of the supply.
statements.B: The diode is an ohmic device because its current increases with applied voltage.
statements.C: The reverse resistance of the diode is very high compared with its forward resistance.
statements.D: Beyond the knee voltage, the forward current rises steeply, almost exponentially.
statements.E: An ordinary diode can be operated safely beyond its reverse breakdown voltage.

solution.key_concept: The diode is non-ohmic, with low forward and very high reverse resistance. Exceeding the breakdown voltage damages an ordinary diode.
steps: A is true by the definition of forward bias.
B is false: the I-V curve is non-linear, so the diode is non-ohmic.
C is true: reverse resistance is very high.
D is true: the current rises almost exponentially beyond the knee.
E is false: exceeding the reverse breakdown voltage damages an ordinary diode.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) leaves out the true statement D. Options (2) and (3) include a false statement (B or E).
solution.common_trap: Thinking that 'current increases with voltage' makes the diode ohmic. Ohmic behaviour requires a linear I-V relation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage
questions.question: A Zener diode is used as a voltage regulator. In which region of its characteristic curve is it operated for this purpose?
options: Forward bias, below the knee voltage
Reverse bias, in the breakdown region
Forward bias, beyond the knee voltage
Reverse bias, below the breakdown voltage

solution.key_concept: A Zener diode is designed to work in reverse breakdown. There the voltage across it stays nearly constant at $V_Z$ over a wide range of current.
steps: In reverse bias, the current is negligible until the voltage reaches $V_Z$.
At $V_Z$, the current rises sharply while the voltage stays almost constant.
This constant voltage over a wide current range is what makes voltage regulation possible.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Reverse bias, in the breakdown region
solution.why_not_others: In forward bias, the Zener diode behaves like an ordinary diode and does not hold its voltage at $V_Z$. Below breakdown in reverse bias, the current is negligible, so no regulation takes place.
solution.common_trap: Expecting a Zener diode to regulate in forward bias, because its forward curve also looks steep beyond the knee.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the pairing: Zener regulation means reverse breakdown plus a series resistor.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage
questions.question: A Zener diode with $V_Z = 6\ \text{V}$ is used in a regulator circuit fed by a $15\ \text{V}$ supply. The total current drawn through the series resistor (Zener current plus load current) is $30\ \text{mA}$. What is the value of the series resistance?

solution.key_concept: The series resistor drops the excess voltage: $R_s = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{I}$, where I is the total current through it.
steps: Voltage across the series resistor: $V_{in} - V_Z = 15 - 6 = 9\ \text{V}$.
solution.why_not_others: $500\ \Omega$ comes from using the full $15\ \text{V}$. $200\ \Omega$ comes from using $V_Z$ alone. $700\ \Omega$ comes from adding $V_Z$ to $V_{in}$ instead of subtracting it.
solution.common_trap: Dividing the supply voltage by the current without subtracting the Zener voltage.
solution.time_saving_tip: Volts divided by milliamperes gives kilo-ohms directly: $9/30 = 0.3\ \text{k}\Omega$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage
questions.question: In a Zener regulator, the input voltage is $20\ \text{V}$, the Zener voltage is $8\ \text{V}$, the series resistance is $400\ \Omega$ and the load resistance is $1\ \text{k}\Omega$. What is the current through the Zener diode?

solution.key_concept: $I_Z = I - I_L = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_s} - \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$
steps: Total current: $I = \frac{20 - 8}{400} = 0.030\ \text{A} = 30\ \text{mA}$.
Load current: $I_L = \frac{8}{1000} = 8\ \text{mA}$.
Zener current: $I_Z = 30 - 8 = 22\ \text{mA}$.
solution.why_not_others: $30\ \text{mA}$ is the total current through $R_s$. $8\ \text{mA}$ is the load current. $38\ \text{mA}$ comes from adding the load current instead of subtracting it.
solution.common_trap: Taking the whole series-resistor current as the Zener current and forgetting the current that flows through the load.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find the current through $R_s$ first, then subtract $V_Z/R_L$.

questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A Zener diode regulates voltage when it is operated in forward bias, in the same way as an ordinary diode.
statements.R: The forward characteristic of a Zener diode is similar to that of an ordinary p-n junction diode.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: A Zener diode regulates only in reverse breakdown. Its forward characteristic is simply like that of an ordinary diode.
steps: Regulation needs the voltage to stay constant at $V_Z$, and this happens only beyond reverse breakdown.
So A is false.
The notes state that the forward characteristic of a Zener diode is like that of an ordinary diode, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) cannot be correct.
solution.common_trap: Expecting a Zener diode to regulate in forward bias.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In a Zener regulator kept in breakdown, if the load resistance is decreased while the input voltage and series resistance stay unchanged, the current through the Zener diode decreases.
statements.II: The Zener voltage $V_Z$ is read from the part of the reverse characteristic where the current remains negligible as the reverse voltage is increased.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $I = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_s}$ stays fixed, and $I_Z = I - \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$. $V_Z$ is read from the vertical (sharply rising current) part of the reverse curve.
steps: $V_{in}$, $V_Z$ and $R_s$ are fixed, so the total current I is constant.
Decreasing $R_L$ increases $I_L = V_Z/R_L$, so $I_Z = I - I_L$ decreases. Statement I is correct.
Where the current is negligible, the diode is still below breakdown.
$V_Z$ is read where the current rises sharply at nearly constant voltage. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II describes the pre-breakdown region, so options (1) and (4) fail. Statement I follows directly from the regulator formula, so option (2) fails.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the Zener current rises when the load draws more current. In fact, the fixed total current is shared, so the Zener's share falls.

questions.topic: Identification of diode, LED, resistor and capacitor from a mixed collection
questions.question: While testing components with a multimeter in resistance mode, a student finds one component that shows the same steady, finite resistance when the leads are connected either way. This component is a

solution.key_concept: A resistor shows the same finite resistance in both directions, with no change over time.
steps: The resistance is steady and does not change with time, so it is not a capacitor.
It is the same in both directions, so it is neither a diode nor an LED.
Therefore the component is a resistor.
solution.why_not_others: A diode and an LED conduct in one direction only. A capacitor shows a transient deflection that decays to very high resistance.
solution.common_trap: Confusing a capacitor's initial deflection with a steady resistance reading.

questions.question: A two-terminal component connected to a multimeter in resistance mode first shows a large deflection. The deflection gradually falls until the reading becomes very high resistance. When the leads are reversed, the same behaviour is seen again. The component is a

solution.key_concept: A capacitor allows a momentary charging current that decays to zero, and this happens in either direction.
steps: A large deflection that decays to very high resistance shows charging.
The transient repeats when the leads are reversed, so the behaviour is not one-way.
This matches a capacitor.
solution.why_not_others: A resistor gives a steady reading that does not decay. A diode and an LED conduct steadily in one direction only and show high resistance on reversal; an LED would also glow.
solution.common_trap: Mistaking the high final reading for diode-like reverse blocking, and ignoring that the transient appears in both directions.

questions.topic: Identification of diode, LED, resistor and capacitor from a mixed collection
questions.question: When a mixed collection of components is tested with a multimeter, which observation distinguishes an LED from an ordinary diode?
options: It emits light while conducting in the forward direction
It shows low resistance in one direction and very high resistance on reversal
It shows the same resistance in both directions
It shows a deflection that decays with time in both directions

solution.key_concept: An LED behaves like a diode but also glows when forward biased.
steps: Both a diode and an LED show one-way conduction, so that test alone cannot tell them apart.
Only the LED emits light when forward biased.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): It emits light while conducting in the forward direction
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is common to both the diode and the LED. Option (3) describes a resistor. Option (4) describes a capacitor.
solution.common_trap: Choosing one-way conduction, which identifies the diode family but does not separate an LED from a diode.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Same steady finite resistance in both directions

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Conducts in one direction only, with no light

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Conducts in one direction only and glows

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Momentary current that decays to zero in either direction

solution.key_concept: Multimeter signatures: resistor gives a steady, two-way reading; diode conducts one way without light; LED conducts one way with light; capacitor shows a decaying transient both ways.
steps: A: a steady reading in both directions means a resistor (III).
B: one-way conduction without light means a diode (IV).
C: one-way conduction with light means an LED (II).
D: a decaying transient in both directions means a capacitor (I).
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the resistor and diode. Option (2) swaps the diode and LED. Option (3) swaps the resistor and capacitor.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the diode and LED, since both show one-way conduction.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix C as the LED (only it glows) and D as the capacitor (only it decays). This removes options (2) and (3) at once.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Identification of diode, LED, resistor and capacitor from a mixed collection
questions.question: Which of the following statements about identifying components with a multimeter are correct?

statements.A: A diode shows low resistance in one direction and very high resistance when the leads are reversed.
statements.B: A capacitor shows a steady finite resistance that is the same in both directions.
statements.C: An LED glows when it is forward biased during the test.
statements.D: After a capacitor has charged and shows very high resistance, reversing the leads produces the decaying deflection again.
statements.E: A component with many terminals is likely to be an integrated circuit.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Each component has a distinctive multimeter signature. An IC is recognised by having many terminals.
steps: A is correct: a diode conducts in one direction only.
B is incorrect: a steady, equal reading in both directions is a resistor. A capacitor shows a transient that decays to very high resistance.
C is correct: an LED glows when forward biased.
D is correct: the transient reappears when the leads are reversed.
E is correct: an IC has multiple terminals.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, C, D and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (2) include the false statement B. Option (3) leaves out the correct statement D.
solution.common_trap: Thinking a charged capacitor stays at high resistance after the leads are reversed, and so rejecting D.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spotting B as false removes options (1) and (2) immediately.
